records.functionAndUse: These records were created by the Department of State in preparation for sending U.S. delegations to international conferences.
otherTitles: Office Files Relating to International Conferences

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of lists of U.S. delegations to international conferences and telegrams, airgrams, letters, position papers, and reports relating to international conferences. Conference topics include food and agriculture; aviation; telecommunications; broadcasting; economic, social, and cultural development; tariffs and trade; medicine, health, and sanitation; fishing, whaling, and other maritime activities; geography and history; intellectual property; education; meteorology; labor; aids to navigation; nuclear energy; tourism and travel; and urbanization.

Included are records relating to the Aero-Medical Association; the American International Institute for the Protection of Childhood; the American National Red Cross; the Associated Country Women of the World; the Australia, New Zealand, United States Security Treaty (ANZUS); the Baghdad Pact; the Cannes Film Festival; the Caribbean Commission; the Census of the Americas (COTA); the Chaco Peace Conference; the Chicago World's Fair; the Colombo Plan; the Conference on the Uses of Radioisotopes in Animal Biology and the Medical Sciences; the Council of Foreign Ministers (CFM); the Danube Commission; the Emergency Advisory Committee for Political Defense; the European Organization for Experimental Photogrammetric Research (OEEPE); the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO); the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT); the Inter-American Association of Broadcasters; the Inter-American Bar Association; the Inter-American Commission of Women; the Inter-American Conference for the Maintenance of Peace; the Inter-American Defense Board; the Inter-American Economic and Social Council (IA-ECOSOC); the Inter-American Nuclear Energy Commission (IANEC); the Inter-American Port and Harbor Conference; the Inter-American Statistical Institute; the Inter-American Travel Congress; the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission; the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (ICEM); the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees; the Intergovernmental Copyright Committee; the Intergovernmental Maritime Consultative Organization (IMCO); the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC); the International Activities Fund; the International Astronomical Union (IAU); the International Authority of the Ruhr (IAR); the International Bureau of Weights and Measures; the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO); the International Conference of Social Work; the International Conference of the Red Cross; the International Conference on Public Education; the International Congress Against Alcoholism; the International Congress of Actuaries; the International Congress of Administrative Sciences; the International Congress of Photogrammetry; the International Congress of Radiology; the International Congress of Refrigeration; the International Congress of Soil Science; the International Congress of the History of Art; the International Congress of Zoology; the International Congress on Tropical Medicine and Malaria; the International Cotton Advisory Committee; the International Council for Large Electric Systems (CIGRE); the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea; the International Council of Scientific Unions; the International Dairy Congress; the International Federation of Agricultural Producers; the International Federation of Women Lawyers; the International Film Festival; the International Geographical Union; the International Labor Organization (ILO); the International Monetary Fund (IMF); the International Poliomyelitis Conference; the International Radio Consultative Committee (CCIR); the International Railway Congress; the International Rice Commission; the International Scientific Radio Union; the International Seed Testing Association; the International Silk Congress; the International Sugar Council; the International Telecommunication Union (ITU); International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee (CCITT); the International Telegraphic Advisory Committee (CCIT); the International Telephone Advisory Committee (CCIF); the International Theatre Institute; the International Union against Tuberculosis; the International Union of Crystallography; the International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics; the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry; the International Union of Pure and Applies Physics; the International Whaling Commission; the International Whaling Conference; the International Wheat Conference; the International Wheat Council; the Japanese Peace Conference; the New York World's Fair; the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO); the North Pacific Fur Seal Commission; the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD); the Organization of American States (OAS); the Organization of the Islamic Conference (OIC); the Pan African Congress; the Pan American Consultation on Cartography; the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO); the Pan American Highway Congress (PAHC); the Pan American Institute of Geography and History Archives Committee; the Pan American Sanitary Organization (PASO); the Pan American Union; the Port-au-Prince Exhibition; the Radio Technical Commission for Marine Services; the Texas Centennial; the Tripartite Conference on the Suez Canal; the United Nations (UN); the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF); the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS); the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC); the United Nations Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East (ECAFE); the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (ECE); the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA); the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA); the United Nations Refugee Fund (UNREF); the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA); the Universal Postal Union (UPU); the U.S. Coronado Exposition Commission; the West Indian Conference; the World Assembly of Youth; the World Food Conference; the World Forestry Congress; the World Health Organization (WHO); the World Meteorological Organization (WMO); the World Petroleum Congress; the World Power Congress; the World's Poultry Congress; and the World Tobacco Congress.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of records of the 20th session of the South Pacific Commission, which was held at Noumea, and dealt with a variety of issues.  Issues covered in the records include health education, nutrition and diet, mosquito-borne diseases, maternal and child health, relations with specialized agencies of the United Nations and other organizations and institutions, agricultural extension and education, publications in the health field, the social development program, literature promotion, audio-visual aids, literacy and territorial library development, education, women and their interests, the Pacific Islands broadcast recordings service, promotion of applied research, fisheries, plant collection and introduction, pests and diseases of plants and animals, the coconut industry, and interterritorial trade promotion.  Included are United States delegation documents dealing with background information, proceedings, working papers and secretariat documents as well as the report of the United States delegation.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of files maintained by Ellsworth Bunker while he served as a consultant to the Department of State, United States Representative to the Council of the Organization of American States (OAS), and Ambassador-at-Large. The bulk of the material pertains to the diplomatic efforts to mediate a settlement to civil war in the Dominican Republic during 1965-1966. 

These records contain substantial information on the politics, culture, and economy of the Dominican Republic and the inner workings of the OAS. Included is information on the initial military intervention by forces of the United States; newspaper articles on various aspects of the occupation; biographical information on key players from the United States and the Dominican Republic; records reflecting press conferences, interviews, public speeches, and official statements from Ambassador Bunker; reports from missions and study groups sponsored by the OAS; proposals and counter-proposals offered by the warring factions; various civil claims filed against the Government of the United States by Dominican nationals; photographs of Ambassador Bunker performing official duties; summaries of meetings with the provisional government; pro-democracy literature produced and distributed by the United States; financial assessments of the expenditures incurred by the United States; and official documents and declarations stemming from the final negotiated settlement which led to the free presidential elections of June 1, 1966, won by Dr. Joaquin Balaguer. 

Additional topics covered include: labor and social unrest initiated by segments of Dominican society; food, clothing, medicine, and other supplies distributed to the local population; matters involving the Inter-American Peace Force (IAPF) composed of troops from Brazil, Honduras, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Paraguay, and the United States; fact-finding tours of the island by American officials; the running of the "Get-Out-The-Vote-Campaign" for democratic elections; the status of election campaigns waged by Dominican candidates for the office of President; and granting of political asylum to foreign nationals.
records.title: Files of Ambassador-at-Large Ellsworth Bunker

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of interrogation reports and memorandums relating to the status of the Communist government and military in China. The reports are divided into two types: "CHARITY" and "UPLIFT" reports. The "CHARITY" reports are summaries of interviews with non-Chinese tourists, businessmen, missionaries, white Russian emigrants, and other sources concerning information regarding areas of China inaccessible by foreign nationals, military forces, rail and airstrip construction, and the situation in certain cities. The "UPLIFT" reports are interrogations of Chinese nationals fleeing Communist rule concerning the situation of life and Communist government policies in major cities, notably Shanghai, as well as the concern of Soviet forces assisting China with military aid and personnel. Also included are memorandums covering the extent of interrogations in Hong Kong and the dissemination of information.
records.title: Hong Kong Interrogation Reports

generalNotes: The Air Coordinating Committee (ACC) was composed of three divisions; Technical, Economic and Industrial.  Under the Technical Division were the following five subcommittees: Aids to Air Navigation and Landing, Aviation Meteorology, Airspace, Air Safety, and Aeronautical Charts.  Under the Economic Division were the following four subcommittees: Facilitation of International Civil Aviation, Area Aviation Policy, Financial Air Services, and Aviation Information and Statistics.  Under the Industrial Division were the following two subcommittees: Aircraft Production and Aviation Research.  In addition to the three divisions, the ACC also established a  so-called "PICAO Panel" to review and coordinate its work with the Provisional International Civil Aviation Organization (PICAO).

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series contains reports, telegrams, correspondence, memorandums, clippings, and policy papers pertaining to relations between the United States and the British islands of Seychelles, Diego Garcia, and Mauritius.  Topics covered include Mauritius' independence from Great Britain in 1968, as well as Seychelles and Diego Garcia's ongoing status as British possessions during this period.  There is information on social, political, and economic conditions on the islands, including diplomatic relations with neighboring states, cultural and educational exchange programs with the West, economic assistance from international lending institutions, mutual defense and internal security programs, improvements to the infrastructure, and industrial development.  Soviet and Chinese communist influences in these regions are also discussed.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence, bulletins, memoranda, periodicals, publications, notes, and reports relating to a number of informal working groups set up by Joseph E. Slater, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs.  Participants in the informal working groups include members of collegiate academia throughout the U.S., U.S. government and non-government workers and consultants, as well as members of various international organizations. Individual working group titles include the Application of Technology to Education and Cultural Affairs, Publishing and Printed Materials Abroad, The Arts and Humanities, Educational and Cultural Advancement in Africa, Educational and Cultural Advancement in Asia, Educational and Cultural Advancement in Latin America, Educational and Cultural Advancement in Atlantic Communities, Educational and Cultural Advancement in Eastern Europe, Educational and Cultural Advancement in the Sino-Soviet Bloc, among others.  Members of the working groups collaborated to develop concepts and feasible means of fostering education and cultural exchange in underdeveloped nations. Included are records relating to the educational and cultural improvement of underdeveloped countries such as Egypt, Algeria, South Africa, Japan, India, China, Ecuador, Argentina and Colombia.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series contains correspondence, telegrams, airgrams, memorandums, circulars, pamphlets, logs, newsletters, clippings, press releases, reports, speeches, statements, hearings, scripts, dispatches, programs, manuals, and lists. The records were collected by Charles Alphonso Smith, the Deputy Special Assistant for Mutual Security Information, and maintained by the Mutual Security Information Staff. The main correspondents include the International Cooperation Administration (ICA), the U.S. Information Agency (USIA), organizations, committees, the United Nations (UN), publishers, and other offices in the Department of State. 

Subjects covered include increasing public understanding of foreign aid fund programs, the mutual security program, the development loan fund, conferences, conventions, transportation, economics, literature, comments on news articles, health, and agriculture. Other topics include ICA and USIA programs; relations between ICA and USIA; the "Around the World Tour" that included Paul Simon, a Representative in the Illinois House of Representatives, other members of the Illinois State Legislature, and newspaper reporters; trips to promote mutual security programs by Charles Alphonso Smith and Leonard J. Saccio the Deputy Director of ICA; and publications and audiovisual materials spread abroad.

Some organizations mentioned in the articles include the American Korean Foundation, the Committee for International Economic Growth, the International Development Advisory Board (IDAB), the National Academy of Sciences, and the Operations Coordinating Board (OCB).
records.title: Subject Files of Charles Alphonso Smith

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of reports, correspondence, memorandums and telegrams and concern international maritime law. There is information on basic principles and judicial concepts involving the Law of the Sea, including the conservation and management of the oceans and its resources, routine shipping and transportation through territorial waters and canals, navigation and signaling on the high seas and inland waterways, passage restrictions on foreign warships and merchant vessels, resolving border disputes and rights of passage through closed seas, safety protocols designed to prevent accidents and ship collisions, provisions of naval honors and ceremonies, national and international regulations governing commercial fishing and deep sea mining, fly over restrictions and air space above territorial waters, ports and harbor facilities open to foreign vessels, combating piracy, trading of enslaved persons and drug smuggling, exploration and international law in the Antarctica, pollution and the dumping of waste in the high seas, international organizations involved in oceanographic research, and lastly, the arrest, detention and impoundment of crews and cargoes. There are also numerous summaries of proceedings from international Law of the Sea conferences, many of which were held in Geneva.
records.title: Law of the Sea Files

This series consists of the personal and professional papers of Foreign Service Officer Martin Joseph Hillenbrand. Included are official correspondence, telegrams, reports, memorandums, background documents for speeches, briefing materials concerning German and Soviet relations, newspaper clippings, and other records relating to his time serving in various foreign service roles, including Vice Consul in Zurich, Switzerland, Consul in Bremen, Germany, First Secretary-Consul to the U.S. Embassy, France, Director of the Office of German Affairs, Deputy Chief of Mission to the U.S. Embassy, Germany, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Hungary, Assistant Secretary of State for European and Eurasian Affairs, and Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Federal Republic of Germany. This series also contains personal writings, including correspondence and documents relating to his doctoral dissertation.

Some records are in German.

These records were maintained by the U.S. Embassy, Federal Republic of Germany from 1972 to 1976; by the Bureau of European Affairs from 1969 to 1972; by the U.S. Embassy, Hungary from 1967 to 1969; by the U.S. Embassy, Federal Republic of Germany from 1962–1967; and by the Office of German Affairs from 1956–1962.
records.title: Files and Papers of Ambassador Martin J. Hillenbrand

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of telegrams, reports, correspondence, memoranda, newspaper clippings, maps, photographs, and other records relating to the program activities of the Office of Refugee and Migration Affairs.  Included are records relating to the history and background of the program; visa and immigration matters; program operations; resettlement of refugees, in particular refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos from the Vietnam War, and Czechoslovakia from the Czechoslovakian crisis (also known as the Prague Spring); special projects; the credentialing of ambassadors and consular generals; political activities; and other economic, financial, health, scientific, and labor matters.  Also included are records relating to the activities of the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (ICEM), the Provisional Intergovernmental Committee for the Movement of Migrants from Europe (PICMME), the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Some records are in Albanian, Arabic, Bulgarian, Chinese, Croatian, French, German, Russian, and Spanish.

records.scopeAndContentNote: Soon after Colombia and the United Provinces of Central America seceded from Spain and established themselves as independent nations, the question of determining their common boundaries arose.  A series of treaties failed to permanently establish boundaries. In 1880 Colombia and Costa Rica concluded an arbitration treaty. That treaty and a second arbitration treaty proved fruitless.  Then on December 4, 1896, a third arbitration treaty was concluded naming the President of France as Arbitrator.  Under this agreement, President Emile Loubet handed down his decision on September 11, 1900. Costa Rica was not satisfied with the decision, but Panama, after declaring independence from Colombia, recognized the Loubet decision.  Now the dispute was between Costa Rica and Panama. After several unsuccessful attempts at settlement, arbitration was agreed upon.  Chief Justice of The United States, Edward D. White was asked to arbitrate.  The arbitration agreement, signed on March 17, 1910, provided for the submission of the following question to the Chief Justice of the United States- "What is the boundary between Panama and Costa Rica under and most in accordance with the correct interpretation and true intention of the award of the President of the French Republic made on the 11th of September 1900?". A Commission of Engineers was established with four survey parties to explore the disputed area.  At the conclusion of its work, the Commission issued a four volume final report.  The first three volumes are with the arbitration textual records (see Inventory NC-155, entry 66) and volume four, a photographic report, is with still picture records (see Record Group 76, series CR). On September 12, 1914, Justice White rendered an award favorable to Costa Rica.  Panama refused to accept his decision.  The outbreak of World War I, however, prevented a timely resolution of this new disagreement. The photographs in this series weretaken by the Commission of Engineers and identified as "worth printing, but not incorporated" in volume four.  The majority of photographs are routine views of disputed areas surveyed in the vicinity of the Sixaola River. There are also several photographs of survey party members, survey camps, and native workers. Corresponding negatives for the prints in this series are in series 76-CP.
records.title: Photographs Taken by the Commission of Engineers, Costa Rica - Panama Boundary Arbitration

records.scopeAndContentNote: These 5"x11" prints are from the Consulate General's Office of the Foreign Service Post of the Department of State.  Photographs were donated by the widow of Walter A. Foote, U.S. Counsel General in Batavia, Java, 1934-47.  There are prints of Japanese political indoctrination programs; which were aimed at the people of Indonesia during World War I.  With English captions these prints cover such topics as the military training of Indonesian youths, the establishment of an Indonesian national government under Japanese occupation, and Japanese and Indonesian cooperation.  Also included in this collection there are photographs of samples of occupation currency and identity cards and photographs of Ir. Soekarno, Prime Minister of the Indonesian Republic.  There are no corresponding negatives.

onlineResources.note: The Department of State Foreign Service records classification manual can be used to determine the file codes for specific files within this series.

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series contains the general working files of the U.S. Consulate, Belem, Brazil. The files typically consist of instructions, despatches, telegrams, memoranda, reports, and other correspondence with the Department of State in Washington; notes to and from the host government; telegrams and despatches to and from other United States embassies and consulates; and letters and other correspondence with private individuals and businesses. Subjects covered may include the internal political, economic, governmental, and social affairs of the host country; Consulate efforts on behalf of United States citizens and businesses; immigration to the United States; trade; the bilateral relations of the United States and the host country; and any subject which consular officials felt might impact the interests of the United States. The files also may include information on internal operations and organization of the Consulate.

findingAids.note: There is a copy of the Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) Filing Manual in the first file of the series.

otherTitles: Switzerland, U.S. Representative to the Economic Commission for Europe, Geneva; Classified and Unclassified Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) and Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) Files

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series contains correspondence, telegrams, airgrams, postcards, memorandums, agendas, notes, press releases, reports, schedules, meeting minutes, agreements, maps, employment applications, clippings, photographs, organization charts, engineering drawings, resolutions, working parties papers, programs, transcripts of speeches, and brochures maintained by the U.S. Delegation to the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) at Geneva, Switzerland. 

The main correspondents include the Department of State, United Nations European Office, U.S. Embassies, U.S. Legations, the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), the United States Congress, the Department of Commerce, ECE delegates from other nations, ECE working groups, the International Authority for the Ruhr (IAR), the Office for the U.S. High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG), the International Road Federation, the Bipartite Control Office Transportation Group, transportation organizations, other U.S. government agencies, organizations, and private industries.

Subject covered include ECE's origin, committees, meetings, schedules, delegates, working parties, finances, policies, administrative issues, and organizational structures; the U.S. Delegation to ECE's establishment of an office in Geneva, housing, administrative issues, personnel, biographical information on staff, finances, and reasons to support ECE; and nations' opinions on issues before the ECE, concerning ECE committees and ECE actions.

Other subjects covered include energy, transportation, railroads, ships, roads, trade, coal, radio traffic, steel, power, industries, agriculture, timber, the Marshall Plan, communications, propaganda, inland waterways, transportation of perishable foods, energy, fuel, labor, railroad restitutions, economics, reports on conversations, relationships between nations, summaries on issues in the press, transportation in Africa, the World Road Conference of 1949, and the ECE Grain Conference.

Some of the organizations and committees discussed include the Mission for Economic Affairs (MEA), the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe (EECE), the Organization for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC), the Office of the Special Representative in Europe (OSR), the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), the European Recovery Plan (ERP), the Association of American Railroads, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Authority for the Ruhr (IAR), the Inland Transport Committee (ITC), the Nederlandsche Internationale Wegvervoer Organisatie (NIWO), the Commission des Echanges de Wagons (CEW), the Central European Wagon Exchange Commission (CEWEC), the Inland Water Transport (IWT), the Office of Military Government U.S for Germany (OMGUS), and the International Road Transport Union (IRU).

The maps include railroads, roads, and tunnels in Africa, Europe, Germany, Italy, Greece, and Turkey.  Some documents are in French or Italian.

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence, memorandums, telegrams, and other documents maintained by the U.S. Consular Court, Tangier, Morocco. Some of the files concern the operation of the court, such as lists of eligible associates to assist the judge at the Consular Court and a file on alleged violations of traffic regulations by and automobile accidents involving U.S. government personnel. Other files concern cases of the court, although the number of documents relating to each case is usually small. Exceptions to this are the case against Sidney Paley, convicted by the Consular Court of aiding and abetting robbery on the high seas and the conspiracy to commit the crime of robbery on the high seas, and a property dispute involving Isaac Fhima.

otherTitles: Index to Records of Diplomatic Posts
Sweden, U.S. Legation, Stockholm; Index to Diplomatic Records for Sweden

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series contains index cards created or maintained by the U.S. Legation, Sweden. The cards partially index correspondence, despatches with the Department of State, notes with the Foreign Office, and miscellaneous records. The cards include some of the following types of information dates, subject lines, personal names, organizations, correspondents, Department of State foreign service post decimal classification scheme numbers, types of document, document numbers, locations, and brief descriptions. Some records in this series partially index the series "United States Diplomatic Records for Sweden, 1818-1936" (ARC Identifier 657249) and "General Records, 1936-1963" (ARC Identifier 1871965).

Some subjects in the indexes to correspondence, despatches, instructions and notes with the Foreign Service covered include transportation, conferences, congresses, communism, international trade, economics, politics, military issues, passports, visas, policies for managing legation affairs, finances, citizenship, official visits, requests for information, laws, Sweden's monarchs, education, and other subjects which legation officials felt might impact the interests of the United States.

The index to miscellaneous records indexes correspondence with the British Legation, correspondence with the U.S. Consulate, Malmo, and reports. Subjects in the index to miscellaneous records include politics, visas, military issues, economics, international trade, official visits, social issues, policies for managing the affairs of the U.S. Consulate, Malmo, Sweden, and other subjects which legation officials felt might impact the interests of the United States.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence, memorandums, airgrams, minutes of meetings, agendas, reports, and statistical summaries pertaining to civil aviation matters in Germany. These records were maintained by officials of the U.S. Embassy, Federal Republic of Germany, who served as representatives on the German government's Standing Commission for Coordination of Aviation. Included are agendas and minutes of meetings of the commission and related working papers. Subjects of the records include the number of civil passenger and freight flights into and out of Berlin, "near miss" incidents, and refugee flights.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series contains reports, telegrams, correspondence, clippings, and memorandums created and accumulated by the United States Embassy in Kinshasa (formerly Leopoldville).  Included are records relating to social, political, and economic conditions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and to U.S. relations with the country.  Included as well are records relating to the programs and policies of President Joseph Desire Mobutu (also known as Mobutu Sese Seko), including the creation of the Corps of Volunteers of the Republic, the Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR), and the National Union of Zairian Workers. Included as well are records relating to educational and cultural exchange programs, foreign aid and military assistance, significant building and construction projects, constitutional reforms and political elections, the DRC's relations with the West and neighboring African states, arrests and prosecution of political opponents, trade and financial agreements, major industries and commodities, backgrounds of leading DRC citizens, visits by foreign dignitaries, social services in provinces and municipalities, major legislation before parliament, and demonstrations, riots and social unrest.  Also included are records relating to personnel and administrative matters at the American embassy and consulates, conferences and meetings with government officials, improvements and maintenance of the grounds and facility, official ceremonies and social affairs, and activities of United States citizens visiting or residing in the region.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of telegrams, correspondence, reports, and memorandums from the United States Embassy in Port Louis and pertains to social, political, and economic conditions in the Republic of Mauritius.  There is information on diplomatic relations with the United States and other Western nations, naval operations in the Indian Ocean (notably at the U.S. base in Diego Garcia), political campaigns for parliamentary elections, the independence celebrations of 1968, major construction projects and improvements to the Mauritian infrastructure, trade and commercial agreements with the West and non-aligned nations, educational and cultural exchange programs with foreign countries, biographical data on influential Mauritians, activities of the United States Peace Corps, advances in science and technology, developments in the field of agriculture (notably sugar), visits by celebrities and foreign diplomats, revenue related to the tourists industry, structure of the banking and financial system, production of petroleum and other fuels, international conferences and meetings, communist activity in the region, and armed conflict in the Middle East. There is also information on personnel, budget, and administration at the U.S. Embassy.     

Some of the records are in French.

creators.heading: Office for Emergency Management. Foreign Economic Administration. Bureau of Supplies. Office of the Executive Director. Engineering Service. (11/1943 - 09/27/1945)

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of letters, memoranda, general reports, historical monographs, regional industrialization studies and technical project reports designed to provide technical analysis of the broad production requirements, needed raw materials, equipment needs, and to provide engineering consultation and services to the Foreign Economic Administration (FEA).  The series includes materials on the industrialization in specific fields for quick development in friendly nations with the goal of assisting the Allied cause in supplementing the processing of food and other goods urgently needed for the war effort.  Also included are records that document the FEA's activities with regard to economic warfare and for post liberation planning for the restoration of basic services such as providing electrical power, restoring clean drinking water, supplying coal and other fuels, and restoring major transportation arteries.

The records also include correspondence and reports relating to various technical missions to foreign countries.  These missions were requested by the country and the records deal with organizing these missions, creating useful technical plans, preparing "Handbooks of Economic Information" on the subject area or country, and providing technical advice on the utilization of local resources to assist in the reconstruction.  Some of the countries covered by these records include Ethiopia, Cuba, and China, along with most of the countries formerly under Axis control.   

In addition, the series includes reports and correspondence on engineering services surveys conducted by the FEA.  These surveys studied the damage to local industry done by the war and furnished a yardstick of the devastation left as once occupied areas were liberated.  These reports cataloged the systematic industrial demolition carried out and identified damage to machinery critical to the restoration of essential services.  

The records also include letters, memoranda and project reports relating to the development of specifications for the production of a locomotive for general use in continental Europe.  

Also included are research materials on a project to find and develop substitute and alternative power fuels.  These fuels and alternative power sources include gas generators, the distillation and hydrogenation of coal, the use of oil shale and the fermentation of agricultural, vegetable and fruit products.  The records include correspondence and reports on the production of high grade hydrocarbon fuels from such materials as grains, sugar cane, beets, potatoes, grapes, bananas, palms, timber and associated products that contain sugars and starches.

The records also include reports, memoranda, and correspondence relating to efforts to obtain a reliable source of quinine from Western Hemisphere sources to replace that formerly imported from the East Indies.  The project focused on cinchona bark and focused on technical problems involved in drying the bark and determining the correct chemical changes that occur between harvesting the bark, drying the bark, and storing the bark for shipment.

Also included are correspondence and reports created by the Engineering Service of the FEA relating to efforts to establish a program for training both foreign and American engineers and equip them with the skills necessary for service in foreign nations.  The records include proposed objectives for the training program, both practical and academic, to participate in the industrialization expected after the war.

The records also include reports, memoranda and correspondence relating to a study made by the Engineering Service on the use of composite wood and sheet steel tanks for the effective transportation of liquids, including petroleum products.  The study was aimed at assisting to secure scarce strategic materials and to conserve both men and machines for the labor needed to construct conventional storage tanks.
records.title: Subject Files

records.scopeAndContentNote:
The photographs in this series were produced and collected by the Picture Division and were furnished to other units of the News and Features Bureau and the Overseas Operations Branch of OWI. The photographs were used to illustrate OWI leaflets, booklets, magazines, and other publications and exhibits which were distributed for use overseas.  Arranged into some 300 subject areas, these photographs document the breadth of American activity in the arts, sciences, politics, war production and defense, education, recreation, medicine, architecture, and communications, to name a few. Included are photographs highlighting activities in many U.S. states; activities in U.S. colleges and universities; the role of women in the homefront defense effort; the contributions of African-Americans to American society; war veterans and their adjustment to civilian life; the activities of American youth; the development of the United Nations; and features on activities of the armed services.

Photographs of interest in this series include views of the doomed ocean liner Lusitania (208-LU-64E-9); a celebration of the Armistice ending World War I (208-LU-64E-8); and a series of images, featuring a marionette of Adolf Hitler, urging precautions against "loose talk" (folder 64J).

In addition, there are several groups of photographs representing the "Portrait of America" feature stories produced by the OWI. These photographs, identified by their green caption sheets, were used in OWI publications overseas in order to illustrate a particular subject, individual, or family representative of America's heritage, values, and fighting spirit.

Negatives for many of the photographs in this series may be found in RG 208, Series N.
records.title: Photographs Depicting "Life in the United States"

records.scopeAndContentNote: The Office of War Information (OWI) was established in the Office of Emergency Management (OEM) on June 13, 1942 to coordinate the Government's War Information program.  It assumed the coordinating functions and related records of the OEM Division of Information and Functions and Records of Government Reports (and predecessor Agencies dating from 1933), the Office of Facts and Figures, and the Office of Coordinator of Information Units concerned with foreign propaganda activities. The Office of War Information was terminated December 31, 1945. The overseas operations were transferred to the Department of State; its domestic operations were performed by the Bureau of the Budget until December 1946 when they were assigned to the reconstituted Office of Government Reports (see Record Group 44). This series of photographs was taken or accumulated by the Office of War Information,  Overseas Branch, News and Features Bureau, Magazine Section.  They were shot by commercial and official photographers of the OWI, the U.S. Army, the U.S. Navy, and the U.S. Marine Corps to be used in OWI exhibits and publications. Some photographs were also acquired from official foreign sources as well as other government branches such as the Soil Conservation Service and the Farm Security Administration. The photographs show civilian and military activities, American and foreign personalities and U.S. and allied military personnel. There are views of war industries, museums, architecture, transportation methods, agricultural activities, war related conferences, cities, natural resources and other topics; a few artworks and stage productions are also shown. Notable personalities are President Franklin Roosevelt, President Truman, Vice President Henry Wallace, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, French President  Charles de Gaulle, singer Lena Horne, suffragette Susan B. Anthony and writer Ernest Hemingway. War related conferences include Casablanca, Potsdam, Teheran, and Yalta. Themagazines the photographs were published in were- Victory, Agriculture- Farming; Rural America, The Parade, USA and others.
records.title: Photographs Used in Publications

records.scopeAndContentNote: Established in December, 1942 within the Overseas Operations Branch of the Office of War Information, the News and Features Bureau played a leading role in the America's World War II propaganda effort abroad, designed to promote an understanding of U.S. life, culture, and war aims.  The Bureau's Picture Division was less a picture-creating agency than a picture-gathering as well as disseminating agency, assembling already-existing photographs from a range of sources -- government as well as commercial -- and furnishing the images to other Bureau offices and to the more than 30 OWI Outposts and 35 State Department missions worldwide.  (For a fuller account of the Picture Division, see the 208-AA series description.) Biographical photo resources were particularly useful in the development of the "Profiles" picture-sets and other OWI presentations highlighting American and Allied accomplishments. Accordingly, Picture Division collections included personality files- a very large Notable Personalities file (208-PU), the full fruit of the Division's picture-stockpiling efforts that began in late 1943; a smaller Wartime Personalities file (208-WP); and other still smaller files (i.e., 208-AFP), all arranged alphabetically by the surname of the individual pictured.  (For a fuller account of 208-PU and WP, see the respective series descriptions). Accompanying 208-PU and WP is a joint alphabetical card index, 208-X, probably assembled by the Picture Division Library staff, with later additions by the State Department's Office of International Information and Cultural Affairs, to which the Picture Division holdings were transferred at the end of 1945. The index incorporates approximately 10,950 3"x5" cards, covering some 10,500 separate individuals represented in one or both of the 208-PU and 208-WP series.  Each card, typewritten or handwritten, contains the name of the pictured individual, or, in cases of members of royal families, the national royal group(i.e., Great Britain Royalty). Where the given individual or royal group is represented by images filed in a folder bearing that individual's or group's name, the index card so indicates.  In cases where an especially prominent individual is represented by multiple folders, the index includes a separate card corresponding to each folder title (i.e., Eisenhower, Dwight D. -Africa; Eisenhower, Dwight D. -Germany, Receiving Russian Award; Eisenhower, Dwight D. -In Sicily).  There are scattered cards that contain cross-reference information, pointing either to an alternative listing for the same individual, or to the name of an individual included as a secondary subject in a photograph filed under the heading of the primary personality. In addition to the above, many of the index cards have a check in pencil or pen.  The check indicates that a photograph of the person mentioned on the card can be found in a "group" folder in 208-WP or PU (A to AK, AL to AN,).  The "group" folders usually contain a single photograph of several different individuals and precede those folders in the two print series which bear the names of individuals beginning with the same letter of the alphabet.  For example, there is a card with a check in this index for Mrs. R. L. Ameno.  The print corresponding to the card is in a "group" folder in box 1 of 208-WP marked AM - AN, with numerous other images of persons whose names also fall within this alphabetical range. These group folders precede the folders individually created for persons whose names begin with the letter "A". The cards do not indicate whether the images for a particular individual are located specifically in 208-PU, in 208-WP, or in both series.  For further location guidance, the user must turn to 208-PU box lists (indicating alphabetical sectors covered by each container) and the 208-WP box and folder lists.  These lists are housed in the Record Group Finding Aid filesin the Research Room. As a basic roster of individuals represented in the series, the card index appears to be quite comprehensive.  Comparison of names represented in sample 208-PU boxes with the names included in the index showed an average correspondence rate of 96%; similar tests carried out with sample 208-WP boxes showed an average correspondence rate of 92%.  In short, if an individual does not appear in the card index, the overwhelming likelihood is that the individual will not be represented in either of these photo series. (For connections among the Picture Division biographical print series, the 208-AA and MO subject print series, and the 208-N copy negative series, consult the description for the 208-Z card index).
records.title: Joint Names Index for Notable Personalities (208-PU) and Wartime Personalities (208-WP) Photographic Files

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series contains reports, correspondence, memorandums, faxes, copies of electronic mail, proposals, work plans, minutes, agreements, audits, implementation reviews, evaluations, and other forms maintained by the Bureau for Europe and the New Independent States (EIS), Office of European Affairs. The documents cover U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) grants to promote development, training, and research in European countries. 

Some of the main correspondents include USAID Missions, USAID Office of the Regional Inspector General, USAID Office of European Country Affairs (ECA) in the Bureau for Europe and New Independent States, USAID Office of Democracy and Governance in the EIS, USAID Office of Regional Housing and Urban Development, the USAID Center for Democracy and Governance in the Bureau for Global Programs, foreign government agencies, and other U.S. government agencies.

Some programs supported by the grants include the Democracy Training and Networking Project (DTN), the Local Governance Partnership Program, the Corporate Program Support Grant, the Environmental Sector Reform Grant, the Participant Training Project, the USAID Partners for International Education and Training program, and the Democracy Commission Small Grant Program in Central and Eastern Europe. Subjects covered by the grants include environmental protections, privatization of businesses, social welfare, laws, agriculture, labor, political processes, social reform, technical assistance, private sector development, management, market economies, capitalism, energy efficiency, energy consumption, development of nongovernmental organizations, housing, training, local government, democracy, human resources, policies, health, women in development, and small businesses development.

Some of the institutions that participated in the grants include the Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID), the Barents Group, the Center for Economic Development, the National Democracy Institute for International Affairs (NDI), the World Council of Credit Unions, the Citizens Democracy Corps, the Volunteers in Overseas Cooperative Assistance (VOCA), the Chemonics (Chemonics International), the Energy Restructuring Group, the Institute for Sustainable Communities, the World Environment Center, the International Executive Service Corps (IESC), the Regional Environmental Center for Central and Eastern Europe, the Development Alternatives Incorporated, the Polish Federation of Independent Entrepreneurs, the Land O'Lakes International Development Division, the American Bar Association's Central and East European Law Institute (CEELI), the European Copper Institute, the Polskie Centrum Promocji, the Acurex Environmental Corps, the Environmental Policy and Institutional Strengthening Indefinite Quantity Contract (EPIQ), the International Foundation for Election Systems, the International Republic Institute (IRI), the U.S. Information Agency (USIA), and universities.

Some of the countries covered include Poland, Czechoslovakia, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Latvia, Bulgaria, Albania, and Estonia. Some of the records contain Polish, Czech, and German.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series contains correspondence, reports, memorandums, agreements, and other documents maintained by the Office of European Country Affairs and its predecessors. The records were originally maintained by the Bureau for Near East and South Asia, Office of Near East and North Africa Affairs from January to October 1975.  The Office of Near East and North Africa Affairs in the Bureau for Near East, later the Bureau for Asia had responsibility for the records from October 1975 to 10/1/1979 when they were transferred to the Office of Project Development in the Bureau for Near East. The records were then maintained by the Bureau for Near East, Office of Project Development from 10/1/1979 to ca. 1986. The Office of Project Development in the Bureau for Asia and Near East had responsibility for the records from ca. 1986-ca. 1990. The Office of Project Development in the Bureau for Asia, Near East, and Europe had responsibility for the records from ca. 1990-ca. 1991 when they were transferred to the Office of European Country Affairs in the Bureau for Europe, Regional Mission for Europe. The records were then maintained by the Bureau for Europe, Regional Mission for Europe, Office of European Country Affairs from 1991-1994. The Office of European Country Affairs in the Bureau for Europe and the New Independent States had responsibility for the records from 1994-ca. 2000 when they were transferred to the Bureau for Europe and Eurasia, Office of European Country Affairs. The records document U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) grants for other countries on local developmental and management projects through foreign governments, institutions, or businesses. The grants cover projects for the development of democratic transition/democracy, privatization, agricultural restructuring, energy efficiency, emergency rehabilitation, medical supplies/assistance, municipal infrastructure, housing, humanitarian assistance, and training. Some of the records are in Hungarian, Polish, and Slovak.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of correspondence, memorandums, reports, studies, agreements, evaluations, and other records pertaining to family planning activities undertaken in various countries through agreements and subagreements between the U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) and partnering organizations.  Included are trip reports outlining objectives and findings for visits to various sites, contracts and amendments to contracts, project proposals, project evaluations, and guides for implementing or improving reproductive health services.  Subjects include voluntary sterilizations, maternal and child health, contraceptive services, and natural family planning.

Partnering organizations include EngenderHealth (formerly known as the Association for Voluntary Surgical Contraception (AVSC) International), International Training in Health (INTRAH) at the University of North Carolina, and the Summa Foundation.

Included are records of family planning activities in Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Cambodia, Dominican Republic, Egypt, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guatemala, Guinea, India, Indonesia, Ivory Coast, Jordan, Kenya, Malawi, Mexico, Nepal, Nigeria, Philippines, Russia, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, Turkey, Uganda, Ukraine, and Yemen.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of photographs that reflect the diversity of photographic sources tapped by the United States Information Agency (USIA) in its efforts to define and propagate American values.  In addition to the material from USIA staff camera people and USIA sources abroad, images come from such picture services as Associated Press and Black Star; magazines and newspapers ranging from "Life" to the "Des Moines Register"; the military services as well as civilian government agencies; private organizations ranging from the Red Cross to Standard Oil; and such well-known photo studios as Harris and Ewing of Washington, D.C.

Periodically, this file was culled to remove images no longer needed for USIA picture-reference and supply operations.  Culled images were sent to the National Archives in substantial blocs.  Letters assigned to each subseries signify the order in which each block was received, but because of the nature of the USIA culling, the contents of each group is not necessarily distinguished in strictly chronological terms.  Thus, subseries 306-PS, while containing a preponderance of material from the 1948-1955 period, also has images from as late as 1961; subseries 306-PSA and 306-PSB, while containing a preponderance of material from 1954-1964, also have images from as early as 1948 and as late (in the case of 306-PSA) as 1973; and subseries 306-PSC and 306-PSD, while containing a preponderance of material from 1962-1972, 306-PSC also have images from as early as 1948, and as late as 1976.  Subseries 306-PSD spans 1948 through 1986.  Subseries 306-PSE is a strictly chronological segment, with virtually all images from the 1973-1983 period.

While subseries 306-PS, 306-PSA, and 306-PSB are exclusively black-and-white, 306-PSC and 306-PSD incorporate a very few, widely-scattered color photographs among the dominant black-and-white entries. The color presence grows more prominent in subseries 306-PSE: of the approximately 37,000 total images in that segment, some 18,400 (49 percent) are color. 

Of the combined total of approximately 367,603 images included in this series, some 30,000 focus on notable personalities from the worlds of politics and government, business, religion, education, science and technology, arts and entertainment, and sports.  Standard head-and-shoulders portraits are abundant, along with a variety of ceremonial, meeting, and action shots.  There is extensive coverage of the activities of 10 U.S. Presidents (Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, John Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan, George Herbert Walker Bush, and William "Bill" Clinton) and Vice-Presidents (Alben Barkley, Nixon, Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Spiro Agnew, Nelson Rockefeller, Walter Mondale, George Bush, and Albert "Al" Gore, Jr.).   Also heavily documented are Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, Congressional leaders, Supreme Court Justices, prominent Governors, and other government officials.

Foreign leaders who helped shape East-West relations in the post-World War II era are amply covered, as well -- among them, Winston Churchill, Charles DeGaulle, Joseph Stalin, Nikita Khrushchev, Mao Tse-Tung, Joseph Tito, Fidel Castro, Indira Gandhi, Ferdinand Marcos, and Margaret Thatcher.

In line with the general USIA emphasis on the American "minority progress" theme, many of the mainstream civil rights figures from the 1950s-60s-70s are also included -- from Martin Luther King, Jr. to Shirley Chisholm.  And in line with an overwhelming USIA emphasis on freedom and diversity in American popular culture, this series is well-stocked with portraits of novelists, poets, painters, sculptors, dancers, musicians, actors, and athletes . . . ranging from Jackson Pollock to Linda Ronstandt, and from Robert Frost to Liza Minnelli to Muhammad Ali.

While not principally a news photo file, this series does incorporate coverage of many of the dramatic developments of the post-World War II decades.  There is extensive material, much of it from the armed services, on the Korean and Vietnam conflicts.  Among other high-profile international events, the Berlin Airlift, Hungarian Uprising, Suez Crisis, Cuban Missile Crisis, U.S. intervention in the Dominican Republic, Camp David Peace Accords, and Panama Canal Treaty also receive coverage.

On the domestic side, this series touches on some of the pivotal developments of the civil rights era, from the Montgomery bus boycott to the signing of the Voting Rights Act to the Poor People's Campaign.  Historic Presidential campaigns, decisive political and economic undertakings (such as the War on Poverty), and momentous technological landmarks (including the progress of the space program, from the Mercury and Gemini flights through the Apollo lunar landing and Mariner probes), draw considerable attention.

Quantitatively more significant than the "news" coverage is the background feature material on varied aspects of American civilization.  There is particularly strong emphasis on the fruits of American education at all levels, from nursery schools to vocational schools to universities.  Scientific research activities also receive extensive play, with images from the national atomic energy labs at Oak Ridge, Los Alamos, and Hanford as well as coverage of diverse research and technological application pursuits at General Electric and other corporate facilities.  Numerous views of industrial, mining, forestry, and agricultural work convey the sense of a bustling American economy and a land with limitless natural resources.  Engineering accomplishments -- public buildings, bridges, highway and railroad systems, ports, housing projects -- are also frequent subjects, with captions often driving home the inter-ethnic cooperation angle.  Scenic landscape views from National Parks, along with picturesque glimpses from cities and towns across the country, produce a collective vision of American beauty.

In some cases, the coverage of American life in this series comes in the form of extended picture-stories, whether generated by USIA staff photographers (e.g., Carolyn Ramsey's story on the small-town side of the 1948 Presidential campaign in Baltic, South Dakota), or, in later years, by freelance camera people (e.g., Thaddeus Miksinski's 1982 study of neighborhoods in Baltimore, Maryland).

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of posters produced by the Joint U.S. Public Affairs Office (JUSPAO) for use in psychological warfare activities supporting the Government of South Vietnam (GVN) during the Vietnam War. A few of the posters were produced by JUSPAO's predecessor, the Joint Field Services Center. The poster themes and designs reflect the fierce competition between the two Vietnams, North and South, to "win the hearts and minds" of the South Vietnamese public.

Target audiences include some of Vietnam's ethnic minorities. Accordingly, translations in Khmer, or Cambodian (e.g., 306-VP-5-2361), at least two dialects (Bahnar and Rhade) of the highland Montagnard peoples (e.g. 306-VP-5-984, 306-VP-7-1249), Korean (306-VP-7-1107), and Cham (306-VP-8-2065), accompany the Vietnamese text of some posters. One poster (306-VP-7-1972) contains what may be traditional, pictographic Vietnamese script. A handful of posters are in English (e.g., 306-VP-11-17) and French (306-VP-10-4), and were likely intended for distribution to United States Information Service (USIS) posts outside of Vietnam.

Most of the posters present an arrangement of three to seven black and white photographs on colored blocks of space with accompanying captions and background text in Vietnamese. A few use color photographs (e.g., 306-VP-5-2, 306-VP-7-14). Thirty posters feature color artworks (example 306-VP-8-10, 306-VP-8-1637, 306-VP-10-190). The majority of the photographs used in the posters were likely taken by JUSPAO's staff photographers (most of whom were Vietnamese), although some came from American military sources. None of the photographs or artworks is credited to individuals.

Posters are grouped under ten main themes reflecting JUSPAO propaganda priorities. The theme with the largest poster concentration is "Support Social and Economic Accomplishments," comprising one third of the total item count. This category highlights the activities of socio-economic development cadres sent under the auspices of government's Revolutionary Development program to work alongside rural Vietnamese in building houses, medical centers, roads, wells, bridges, schools, markets, and in making other infrastructure improvements. Many of the rural communities featured were the New Life Hamlets, planned new communities comprised of refugees and other rural people relocated by the GVN from Viet-Cong-controlled areas to pacified districts. 

Another well-represented theme is "Encourage the Goals of the Chieu Hoi Program," referring to the South Vietnamese government program designed to encourage and facilitate the defection of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese soldiers back to the Southern cause (Chieu Hoi meant "to summon back," or more popularly, "Open Arms"). Returnees are shown at the moment of their surrender, sometimes along with weapons they brought in (with statistics concerning defection numbers and weapons yields often accompanying the images). Meant to show the successful re-integration back into South Vietnamese society of returnees, as well as to refute Viet Cong propaganda alleging their ill-treatment, many posters show returnees reaping promised program benefits during their stays at provincial Chieu Hoi centers (cash awards; good, regular food and medical care; reunion with their families; education and vocational training; participation in sports and other leisure activities). Direct appeals to Viet Cong to return to their families, and appeals to family members of Viet Cong to induce their loved ones to defect, appear in the posters, as well as detailed instructions about how and where to surrender. Many former Viet Cong are shown in their new lives, practicing a trade or serving as members of local Popular Forces or armed propaganda teams. 

The "Explain American Presence in Vietnam" grouping illustrates the activities of U.S. military personnel in Vietnam, with the purpose of assuring the rural people of the South of the friendly intentions of the United States. Posters show Americans building and repairing bridges, schools, and houses in the countryside, performing medical examinations and procedures for rural people, and distributing food and other relief items to refugees and poor villagers; in addition, a few posters illustrate American military power. Several posters in this category feature South Korean forces engaged in similar activities. A small number also feature the activities in Vietnam of other allied forces from Thailand, New Zealand, the Philippines and Australia. 

Another large category, "Exploit All Military Victories," publicizes military victories won by Popular Forces, Regional Forces and Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) forces against the Viet Cong. Shown are Vietnamese troops in battle, captured and killed enemy soldiers, captured weapons and facilities, military decoration ceremonies, victory parades, and exhibits of captured enemy equipment. The names of several South Vietnamese military operations are cited in these posters (e.g., Operation Hung Vuong 9, Operation Xay Dung 6, and Operation Cooperation 26). Several top-ranking ARVN officers also appear in posters within this category.

The "Exploit Viet Cong Vulnerabilities" highlights the depredations and atrocities committed by the Viet Cong in the South. Pictures show dead and wounded atrocity victims, funerals of victims, captured Viet Cong perpetrators, buildings damaged and destroyed in Viet Cong attacks, the hardships imposed on the people by Viet Cong actions, and anti-Viet Cong protest rallies. A few posters also relate the story of the Viet Cong defector, Nguyen Van Be, shown holding North Vietnamese newspapers that erroneously announce his sacrifice of his life for the sake of the Northern cause (306-VP-5-1774, 306-VP-5-1847). 

The smaller-volume categories feature hortatory messages on public health issues, Vietnamese armed forces recruitment, and a broad miscellany of subjects that include the U.S. Apollo 11 lunar mission (306-VP-10-5), Vietnamese public security (306-VP-10-224), and the inauguration ceremony for South Vietnamese President Nguyen Van Thieu (306-VP-10-7). Offering a somewhat different narrative approach to the social and economic progress subject, the final category contains seven poster sets (some incomplete) numbering seven to eleven posters each, showing the military and socio-economic development activities of forces from various allied nations, self-help and Revolutionary Development activities in the villages, Viet Cong atrocities, and captured Communist weapons, documents, and enemy soldiers. All of the posters with English captions appear in this category. 

Many of the posters in the smaller-volume categories appear to have been gathered by JUSPAO from other, often unidentified sources. At least one poster (306-VP-8-11) is identified as coming from the "Public Health Education Service, Public Health Division," presumably an agency of the GVN. There are other posters in the public health category that bear the same type of original numbering and have the same design, but are wholly unidentified as to source. 

Several province chiefs, district chiefs, and hamlet chiefs appear in JUSPAO posters, as well as high-ranking GVN members such as Chief of State Nguyen Van Thieu (306-VP-7-14, 306-VP-1-853), Prime Minister Nguyen Cao Ky (306-VP-7-1168, 306-VP-2-1372), Chieu Hoi Minister Nguyen Ngoc and Major General Nguyen Van Minh, Security Chief for Saigon (306-VP-3-2736), and Major General Nguyen Duc Thang, Minister of Revolutionary Development (306-VP-7-1082, 306-VP-7-1398). A historical figure, the 13th-century Vietnamese general Tran Hung Dao, famous for repulsing two successive Mongol invasions, appears along with a poetic rendition of his rousing speech to incite the leaders of Vietnam to expel the Mongol invaders (306-VP-10-190). Shown in posters are a number of high-ranking American government officials, such as President Lyndon B. Johnson (306-VP-1-2746), Vice President Hubert H. Humphrey (306-VP-7-1008), U.S. Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare John Gardner (306-VP-7-1105), U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Arthur Goldberg (306-VP-1-1478), and Governors Clifford Hansen of Wyoming and George Romney of Michigan (306-VP-7-980). 

Other posters of note include a representation of a traditional Vietnamese horoscope calendar with politicized horoscope readings (306-VP-1-915), scenes showing the growth in popularity of the motorbike in Vietnamese life (306-VP-7-2139), and a scene of an American soldier giving help to a distressed refugee family (306-VP-1-1412). There are multiple posters that display numerous mug shots of Viet Cong defectors with information such as name, rank, place of origin, and date of defection (306-VP-3-1120, 306-VP-3-2106).

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series documents the operational and functional activities of the United States Information Agency (USIA).  Memorandums, publications, policy papers, news clippings, telegrams, despatches, agreements, correspondence, research reports, and studies document the informational and cultural activities of the United States Government.  The records in this series describe the agency's mission, policies, organization, and administration from the World War II period to the agency's abolishment in 1999.  The records document the myriad cultural programs implemented by the USIA to transmit American political and cultural values abroad.  The nine subject areas in this series include mission and policy direction, administrative and program support, educational exchanges, broadcast media, print and visual media, programs, overseas operations, international communication and public diplomacy, and predecessor agencies.  

The records in this series pertaining to the mission and policies of the USIA delineate the agency's growth as an independent foreign affairs agency within the executive branch.  In the context of USIA administration, reports, memorandums, and Congressional legislation document the allocation of financial and human resources in the development of a comprehensive informational-cultural program.  This series documents USIA personnel relations and management issues both within the Foreign Service and domestically.

A fundamental part of the USIA's work was the exchange program implemented by the Fulbright - Hays Act in 1961.  The records of the exchange program underscore how the USIA implemented the exchange program to strengthen international understanding and further the national interest of the United States.

In addition to the exchange program, international broadcasting became an essential tool for transmitting American ideas and values.   Studies, reports, and memorandums document the development and expansion of Voice of America (VOA), the USIA's international radio service.  In addition to the Voice of America, the records in this series document the operations of Radio Free Europe, Radio Liberty, Radio Free Asia, Worldnet Television, Radio Marti, and TV Marti.     

The USIA policy of countering negative images of America led to the development of exhibits and fairs during the early 1950s.  News clippings, memorandums, and studies present the Cold War struggle through visual media. The planning and implementation of displays highlighting American creative art was reflected in several exhibitions, most notably, in the Brussels Fair exhibit (1958), the American National Exhibition (1959), and the Montreal Expo (1965).  This series also underscores the role of the USIA film program in seeking to portray American society, policies, and people.

Reports, manuals, news clippings, and correspondence document the programs and overseas operations of the USIA.  Through Arts America, the Artistic Ambassador Program, the Book Program, English Language Teaching Program, and People to People Program, the USIA cooperated with private American institutions and citizens to communicate important aspects of U.S. culture to foreign audiences abroad.   

This series includes records pertaining to USIA binational and cultural centers.   U.S. Information Service (USIS) officers in centers overseas made local arrangements and provided public affairs and logistical support.   Records pertaining to the Joint United States Public Affairs Office (JUSPAO) are in Vietnamese.  

This series also includes reports and correspondence on the Reagan - Gorbachev Summit, held in 1985, and news clippings, reports, and transcripts from the Office of War Information.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of administrative regulations, announcements, catalogs, circulars, correspondence, directives, drafts, guidelines, handbooks, issuances, manuals, memorandums, operating manuals, organizational charts, press releases, procedures, notes, regulations, and reports relating to the creation and updating of the U.S. Information Agency's (USIA) Manual of Operations and Administration (MOA), which covers the administration, organization, policies, and programs of USIA.  The records were maintained by the Management Analysis / Regulations Staff, and its predecessor, the Management Division.

Some of the topics covered include USIA's functions, recordkeeping, benefits, employment in foreign countries, budgets, finances, security, procurement, programming, planning, library services, private cooperation, post management, press services, and staff services. Also described are the domestic and foreign operations for personnel, broadcasting, information centers, Binational Centers (BNC), cultural programs, motion pictures, television, field radios, and communications. The records also include information for creating and updating USIA handbooks that cover topics such as overseas communications; records management; records classifications; time and attendance; overseas finance operations; field radio operations; information centers physical standards; presentations; book translation programs; play productions; and inspections of oversea posts. 

Included are filing manuals used by USIA (file: "CR 19 Part III 500 (I) 1957-1969") and the U.S. Information Service (file "CR 19 Part III 600 1955-1968") in addition to the U.S. International Information Administration (IIA)'s organization manual (file: “Handbook IV-Glossary”).

The U.S. Information Agency's (USIA) Manual of Operations and Administration (MOA) is arranged into seventeen parts, some of which are unassigned or changed to other topics during some years. Part one covers organization and functions of USIA. Part two covers general administration. Part three covers communications, records management, and filing manuals. Part four covers administrative services. Part five covers domestic and foreign personnel services. Part six covers USIA's budget. Part seven covers finances, such as accounting, leave, and attendance. Part eight covers security. Part nine covers procurement regulations for domestic and overseas operations. Part ten covers programming and planning. Part eleven covers broadcasting operations, such as Voice of America (VOA) and radio operations. Part twelve covers information center operations, such as library operations, Binational Centers (BNC), book translation programs, overseas lecture activities, and music programs. Part thirteen covers motion picture and television operations. Part fourteen covers post management including the overseas press and publications practices. Part fifteen covers private cooperation. Part sixteen covers press services, such as post mailing lists, overseas establishments, inspector's handbooks, administration support agreements, and the administration for African posts. Part seventeen covers staff operations and services.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of photographs of Presidents of the United States, First Ladies, Vice Presidents, and Presidential hopefuls. Also featured in this series are images of foreign dignitaries and their visits to the United States as well as Presidential trips abroad and engagements with prominent, international leaders. The first President included in this series is Thomas Jefferson, and it concludes with images of the electoral candidates for the 2000 presidential election. 

Images of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in his youth, as Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Navy (1913 to 1920), and during his Presidential terms are among the records.  Also included are family photographs showing the President and Mrs. Franklin Roosevelt and their children taken in Washington, DC during 1916 and 1919. 

President John F. Kennedy is pictured speaking with groups and dignitaries as well as with family members.  These images also show him with his parents, grandparents, and especially his brothers Robert F. Kennedy and Ted Kennedy.  During the Cuban Missile Crisis on October 29, 1963, Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara is shown at the White House with President Kennedy. 

Included among the oversize items in this series, are engravings of President Rutherford B. Hayes, President Harry Truman, President Dwight D. Eisenhower, and President Kennedy.  President Jimmy Carter is pictured signing the Strategic Arms Limitation Talk II Treaty in Vienna in 1979.   Also, President Bill Clinton is shown with Nelson Mandela, South African civil rights leader and politician.

records.scopeAndContentNote: These files were maintained by the Office of the U.S. Commissioner General to the Universal and International Exhibition of 1967 (Montreal, Quebec). This series consists of letters, memorandums, notes, maps, magazines, magazine articles, pamphlets, newspaper clippings, aerial photographs, photographs, resumes, architectural drawings, blueprints, tourist maps, travel vouchers, plane tickets, correspondence, and budget listings related to the 1967 Universal and International Exhibition in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. The records are mainly from William L. Clark, Deputy U.S. Commissioner General, and John J. Slocum, Assistant U.S. Commissioner General. Other correspondents include the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition; Buckminster Fuller, the architect; and General Dynamics, the designing company. This series covers subjects such as the design of the U.S. Pavilion, the U.S. Pavilion building design competition, the Exhibition budget, and the construction of the electronic, air, and heating systems in the U.S. Pavilion. Also addressed are past World Exhibitions in Brussels, New York, Moscow, Seattle and London; special events at the Exhibition; hiring of guides and employees; the design and architecture of the Soviet Pavilion; the approval of Chicago for the location of the 1976 exhibit; and the final selection of special events at the Exhibition. A few of the records in this series are in French.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of incoming circular letters from the Department of State relating to organizational activities, cultural and educational programs, and U.S. Information Agency (USIA) operations in Latin America. This series contains records pertaining to Argentina, Barbados, Bolivia, Brazil, British West Indies, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Martinique, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Included are communications relating to the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission, U.S. Space program, Peace Corp, Youth Conservation Corps, World Food program, World Youth Forum, Alliance for Progress, and the Law of Treaties Conference. Included are records relating to international travel, citizenship, and passports. Also included in the series are communications relating to cultural and education exchange programs. This includes educational programs relating to English language instruction, foreign scholarships, teacher development, university professor exchange, and Americans abroad. Some of the documents are in Spanish and French.
