records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of correspondence, memorandums and other records relating to organizational activities, cultural and educational programs, and U.S. Information Agency (USIA) operations in Latin America.  It contains records pertaining to Argentina, Barbados, Bolivia, Brazil, British West Indies, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Haiti, Honduras, Jamaica, Martinique, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad, Uruguay, Venezuela, and the West Indies.  Included are memorandums, correspondence, incoming and outgoing telegrams and airgrams, radio broadcast reports, budget reports, financial statements, briefings, circulars, handbooks, press releases, pamphlets, newsletters, inspection reports, and copies of newspaper clippings and magazines.

Topics covered include communist propaganda activities, labor and economic information activities, television and radio broadcasts, and the recruitment and operations of the Peace Corps.  Included are communications relating to binational center programs, Latin American book translation programs, Public Affairs Office (PAO) conferences, Alliance for Progress program, Voice of America radio broadcasts, student exchange programs, Operation UNITAS, English language instruction programs, Country Analysis Strategy Papers (CASP), Country Plan Program Memorandums, and the US Space Program.  Some of the documents are in Spanish.

records.functionAndUse: These records were collected and maintained to document the Director’s daily communication while he worked to fulfill the U.S. Information Agency's mission to understand, inform, and influence foreign publics in promotion of the national interest, and to broaden the dialogue between Americans and U.S. institutions, and their counterparts abroad.

referenceUnitNames: National Archives at College Park - Textual Reference

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence written by Charles Z. Wick while in office as Director of the United States Information Agency (USIA). Correspondence includes copies of letters to a wide variety of people including the President of the United States, the public, members of the chief of staff to the president, staff of the USIA, members of the House of Representatives, Ambassadors to foreign countries, representatives of foreign and domestic publishers and members of the media, and other influential figures. Topics include Soviet propaganda trends, Central American attitudes on U.S. Contra Aid, foreign media reaction to the President’s State of the Union Speech, policy and foreign perceptions reports, cultural exchanges, book publications, speeches given and heard by Wick, foreign and domestic trips taken by Wick, World Net Dialogue Program, the Voice of America, youth exchange programs, USIA International Council invitations, International Information talks. Also included are routine subjects such as thank-you letters, invitations, sympathy letters, best wishes, congratulations, recommendations, and other similar topics.
records.title: Chronological Correspondence Files of Director Charles Wick

This series contains information collected by Heinz Kaufmann, a lawyer in the Tripartite I. G. Farben Control Group's (TRIFCOG) Finance and Accounting Section.

These records detail the size and scope of the I.G. Farbenindustrie A. G. conglomerate and the financial and legal problems involved with its dissolution. Major topics include the relationship of I.G. Farbenindustrie A. G. with Deutsche Landerbank A. G.; the relationship of I. G. records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of records created or accumulated by the Finance, Industry, and Economic Branches of the Economic Affairs Division (EAD) of the Office of the Land Commissioner for Hesse (OLCH) which was a part of the Office of the U.S. High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG) and by the EAD's predecessor, the Economic Affairs Division of the Office of Military Government for Hesse, under the Office of Military Government for Germany, U.S. (OMGUS).

These records document the EAD's comprehensive review and systematic regulation of the economic and financial affairs of the Hessian State Ministry of Finance and of privately owned and state subsidized German industries. This oversight program was undertaken in execution of OLCH's assigned economic functions and responsibilities.

The series covers such subjects as the EAD's review or regulation of the Hessian Finance Ministry accounts relating to: 1) occupation costs incurred by the U.S. Army in Land Hesse; 2) proposed Hessian Finance Ministry fiscal policies and budgetary plans relating to requests for financial equalization  (or OLCH subsidies to compensate for losses in land tax revenues); 3) valuation of previously requisitioned and released real property, and German tax code and currency reform; and 4) claims of German nationals for compensation by the U.S. Government for losses sustained under OMGUS or HICOG occupation. 

The records also document the EAD's systematic survey and evaluation of German industrial development in Land Hesse, particularly the economic progress made in transportation (railroads, highways, and internal waterways), retail trade, and the textile, iron, coal, and automotive industries.

Records include bills, budget submissions, financial statements, laws, letters, memorandums, and reports.
records.title: General Correspondence Relating to the Review and Regulation of Hessian State Economic and Financial Affairs

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of correspondence between national governments and the Office of Military Government for Germany, U.S. (OMGUS) and the U.S. Element of the Extradition Board of the High Commission for Germany regarding alleged war criminals. 

Files generally provide biographical data of a prisoner and a summary of the crime alleged. Some files have letters of support for the defendant; others of condemnation. Other records relate to the case made by the nation requesting extradition. 

Some files contain summary reports that cite the numbers of extraditions requested by a country. Other files (e.g., "98 - Polish - General Folder B") contain lists of those extradited. The files for Austria contain extensive reports that list actions taken in regard to particular extradition requests.

Also included is administrative correspondence regarding travel approval for witnesses.
records.title: War Crimes Correspondence

records.functionAndUse: This series supplements the larger collection of Criminal Case Files, 1949-1955 (ARC ID 1414055); no duplication of case files has been found. This series apparently constitutes case files forwarded to Berlin, possibly for further review by Allied judicial authorities there, and subsequently held at the Berlin Document Center with other administrative materials from the occupation period. It is likely that this series was originally intended for incorporation within the larger series, but their retention in Berlin precluded such action before the closing of the principal OMGUS and HICOG record collections. Both series are necessary for documentation of criminal justice in occupied Germany, 1945-1949.

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of criminal case files in those areas of Germany initially under the authority of the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS) and later under the authority of the United States High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG). Most cases involve displaced persons, usually Poles, Russians, Ukrainians, and other eastern European nationals forcibly deported as slave labor to Germany during the war. Convicted of postwar crimes against German nationals or other displaced persons, these individuals appealed their convictions to OMGUS or HICOG judicial authorities. 

Other cases involve the original jurisdiction of Allied courts including the following categories: German nationals tried by American authorities for the falsification of Fragebogen information or identity papers; incidents involving U.S. military personnel, including traffic accidents and crimes against German nationals; and investigations and trials of American personnel for misconduct in the handling of security-classified records.

Case files usually include a summary charge or cover sheet, original and appellate court documents, and related correspondence. A significant number of the appellate cases include German-language documentation originated by local German police and court authorities. In a few cases, documentation includes personal Wehrmacht or Waffen-SS identity records.

Several cases contain particularly significant documentation that transcend routine criminal proceedings. The case file for Wenzel Hrnecek, a Czech national accused of numerous crimes committed against ethnic Germans while in command of an internment camp in Czechoslovakia, includes extensive information on the treatment of the Sudeten German population by Czech authorities during the period May 1945 - November 1946. The case file for Max Bittner et al. concerns a railway disaster in July 1945 that resulted in the deaths of over 100 persons. A few cases (e.g., Geiger, Emil; Russian Prisoners of War [POWs], Shooting of) involve followup proceedings to war crimes trials and investigations.
records.title: Criminal Case Files Held at Berlin

records.scopeAndContentNote:
This series consists of lists, reports, correspondence, memorandums, staff announcements, minutes and minutes extracts in the general subject files of the Extradition Board. The main subjects covered in this series are Extradition Board policies and policy formulation as well as information on individual extraditions. There are several lists concerning extraditions throughout the series. The lists of individuals extradited to Austria, Belgium, Britain, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Russia, and Yugoslavia provide names and birth dates. The war criminal prisoner data includes name of criminal, date and place of birth, nationality, previous criminal convictions, name of court and place of trial, offense, sentence, clemency, sentence expiration, and a description of the offense. 

The extradition requests and decisions on those requests include a summaries of the case facts and decisions rendered, clearances to extradite certain individuals, and lists of prisoners held. Many announcements, reports and memorandums deal with extradition principles and problems, including legislation needed, the composition of the Board, processing extradition requests, and termination of extradition requests.

Other topics include the legal status of displaced persons from Germany, an explanation of the court system used to try war crimes in the French Zone, British policies, extradition treaties to which Germany was a party in 1939, cases held for tripartite consideration, and extradition and legal assistance between the Federal Republic of Germany and Iron Curtain countries. A small amount of material is in French and German without translation.
records.title: General Subject Files

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence, interrogation reports, questionnaires, and memorandums relating to interrogations of defectors from the Eastern European countries of Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, and the U.S.S.R.  Questions asked in the interrogation vary based on the subject's background and seek information on political, economic, and social events in Eastern Europe.  The interrogation reports often question how the subject received information, particularly about the West.  Files sometimes contain a detailed questionnaire on the subject's radio listening habits.  Some of the specific subjects covered by the interrogations include education, attitudes toward Soviet films, attitudes toward political events, employment conditions, standard of living, agriculture, propaganda, and Soviet controls.

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of audio recordings of speeches given by, and interviews conducted with, directors of various United States foreign assistance agencies. The topics covered generally deal with the overseas economic and technical assistance programs implemented in the years following World War II. Included is a nationally broadcast interview with Harold Stassen, director of the Foreign Cooperation Administration (FCA), in which he discussed State Department and FCA controversies, including those with Senator Joseph McCarthy. In another interview, John Hollister, head of the International Cooperation Administration (ICA) answered questions about foreign aid practices. Also included is a speech given to the Sixth National Conference on International Economic and Social Development by Leonard Saccio, Acting Director of the ICA, titled "ICA and the Immediate Task Ahead."

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of speeches given and talking points used by the Director and other high-level officials of the Trade Development Agency (TDA) at speaking engagements. Records include drafts of remarks, generic speech outlines, presentation outlines, and talking points. Also included are writing samples from a pool of potential speech writers, as well as news releases for speech events and ceremonies. Topics include U.S.-Central Asia: Partnership for Economic Progress, energy development, U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) in Eastern Europe, Ukrainian economy, TDA strategic plan, training projects in Turkey, U.S. technology in East Asia, and others.
records.title: Director's Speech Files

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of correspondence, reports, and photographs regarding international volunteer programs and events associated with the Peace Corps, including the United Nations Volunteer (UNV) Program, International Volunteer Day, and the 1981 Icara Conference on Refugees in Africa. records.scopeAndContentNote: This series consists of electronic calendar and schedule files for the Associate Director for the Office of Volunteer Recruitment and Selection. Calendar files document meetings, appointments, telephone calls, trips, visits, and other activities of the Associate Director. Most calendar items consists of data elements noting the meeting organizer, subject, location, start date, start time, end date, and end time. Some calendar items also include the email addresses and/or names of required attendees and optional attendees, the sent time of an appointment, and a brief description.

referenceUnitNames: John F. Kennedy Library

records.scopeAndContentNote: This series contains newsletters and other periodicals written by Peace Corps volunteers (PCVs) and staff members. While some cover the agency as a whole, the majority were produced by volunteers in the field for distribution to other PCVs in their country or region. Most newsletters appear to have been short-lived, most likely due to the volunteers’ 2-year service term. This collection does not contain complete runs of the titles listed here. There are often only one or two issues of a particular publication present.
records.title: Newsletters and Periodicals
